translationRepairs: She was given in marriage to Xiao Chubou; the annals for the seventh month of Taiping year 7 write Yanmuqin as Nianmigun and do not write Chubou as Choubu.
She was given in marriage to Xiao Chubou; the annals for the seventh month of Taiping year 7 write Yanmuqin as Nianmigun and write Chubou as Choubu.
In 蕭啜不作蕭鉏不 the final 不 belongs to both personal names; 作 equates 蕭啜不 with 蕭鉏不, so the English “do not write … as” wrongly negates the annalistic orthography note.
Given in marriage to Xiao Chubou—per the annals, in the seventh month of Taiping year 7 Yanmuqin is written Nianmigun and Chubou is not written Choubu.
Given in marriage to Xiao Chubou—per the annals, in the seventh month of Taiping year 7 Yanmuqin is written Nianmigun and Chubou is written Choubu.
The same annotation 蕭啜不作蕭鉏不 records that the annals write Chubou as Choubu; literal “is not written” invents a negation absent from 作.
At the end of the Taiping era, when Daling Yan rebelled at the Eastern Capital, she was killed.
At the end of the Taiping era, when Da Yanlin rebelled at the Eastern Capital, she was killed.
東京大延琳反 names the rebel 大延琳 (Da Yanlin); “Daling Yan” mis-segments the three-character personal name.
At the end of Taiping, when Daling Yan rebelled at Eastern Capital, she was killed.
At the end of Taiping, when Da Yanlin rebelled at Eastern Capital, she was killed.
Literal English likewise mis-parses 大延琳 as “Daling Yan”; the source names Da Yanlin as the Eastern Capital rebel.
Imperial Son-in-law Daliqiu was executed for involvement in the Daling Yan affair, and she remarried Xiao Laogu.
Imperial Son-in-law Daliqiu was executed for involvement in the Da Yanlin affair, and she remarried Xiao Laogu.
坐大延琳事 refers to involvement in the Da Yanlin affair; “Daling Yan” is the same misreading of 大延琳.

In the seventh year of the Kaitai era she was enfeoffed Princess of Wei State, advanced to Princess of Qin State, and then titled Princess of Qin-Jin State; at the beginning of the Qingning era she was advanced to grand princess—the epitaph of Miaoxing Dashrishi in Liaowen Hui records her as Grand Princess of Qin-Yue State.

In the seventh year of the Kaitai era she was enfeoffed Princess of Wei State, advanced to Princess of Qin State, and then titled Princess of Qin-Jin State; at the beginning of the Qingning era she was advanced to grand princess—the epitaph of Master Miaoxing in Liaowen Hui records her as Grand Princess of Qin-Yue State.
遼文匯…妙行大師行狀碑 names Master Miaoxing (妙行大師); “Dashrishi” is a corrupt rendering of 大師.
She was enfeoffed Princess of Wu State; at the beginning of the Tonghe era she was advanced to Wei State and then titled Princess of Wei State.
She was enfeoffed Princess of Wu State; at the beginning of the Tonghe era she was advanced to Wey State and then titled Princess of Wei State.
進封衞國，改封魏國長公主 distinguishes 衞 from 魏; the proposal is right to separate them, but English fields may not embed Chinese graphs—Wey vs Wei is the established distinction.
Son of Prince Zhaohuai, one daughter:
昭懷太子一女： states that Prince Zhaohuai had one daughter; “Son of Prince Zhaohuai” invents a son and misreads the kinship head.
She was enfeoffed Princess of Chu State and transferred to Xu State; in the first year of the Qiantong era she was advanced to Princess of Zhao State and titled Princess of Qin-Jin State.

She was enfeoffed Princess of Chu State and transferred to Xu State; in the first year of the Qiantong era she was advanced to Princess of Zhao State and additionally titled Senior Princess of Qin-Jin State.
加秦晉國長公主 adds the 長公主 rank; omitting 長 and saying only “titled Princess” understates both the addition (加) and the senior-princess title.
Enfeoffed Princess of Chu State, transferred to Xu State. In the first year of Qiantong, advanced to Zhao State, added Princess of Qin-Jin State.
Enfeoffed Princess of Chu State, transferred to Xu State. In the first year of Qiantong, advanced to Zhao State, added Senior Princess of Qin-Jin State.
Literal likewise drops 長 from 秦晉國長公主; “Senior Princess” restores the source title rank.

In childhood she suffered during Yixin's persecution and was raised with her brother Tianzuo in Xiao Huaizhong's household. Later Lady Li advanced Jia Guge; Emperor Wen was moved and summoned them back to the palace.

In childhood she suffered during Yixin's persecution and was raised with her brother Tianzuo in Xiao Huaizhong's household. Later Lady Li presented the Jia Guge (Song of Carrying Grain); Emperor Wen was moved and summoned them back to the palace.
李氏進挾穀歌 means Lady Li presented the song 挾穀歌; treating Jia Guge as a person she “advanced” invents an agent and misreads 進…歌.

In youth she suffered Yixin's persecution and, with her brother Tianzuo, was raised in Xiao Huaizhong's household. Later Lady Li advanced with Jia Guge; Emperor Wen was moved and summoned them back to the palace.

In youth she suffered Yixin's persecution and, with her brother Tianzuo, was raised in Xiao Huaizhong's household. Later Lady Li presented the Jia Guge (Song of Carrying Grain); Emperor Wen was moved and summoned them back to the palace.
Literal “advanced with Jia Guge” likewise misreads 進挾穀歌; 進 governs presentation of the song title.

All were captured by the Jin—per the biography of Zongwang in Jin History 74, Tianzuo's daughters taken by the Jin were Guyü, Yuliyan, Woliyan, Da'aoye, and Ci'aoye; only the eldest escaped in the army chaos. Yuliyan is the same as Yuliyan.

All were captured by the Jin—per the biography of Zongwang in Jin History 74, Tianzuo's daughters taken by the Jin were Guyü, Yuliyan, Woliyan, Da'aoye, and Ci'aoye; only the eldest escaped in the army chaos. That Jin History form of Yuliyan is the same as this table's Yuliyan.

餘里衍即余里衍 equates two orthographies of the same name; the proposal correctly flags the collapsed English, but English fields may not embed Chinese graphs—naming the Jin History vs table forms preserves the note.

All captured by Jin—per Jin History, Biography 74 Zongwang, among Tianzuo's daughters captured by Jin were Guyü, Yuliyan, Woliyan, Da'aoye, and Ci'aoye; only the eldest escaped during the army turmoil. Yuliyan is Yuliyan.

All captured by Jin—per Jin History, Biography 74 Zongwang, among Tianzuo's daughters captured by Jin were Guyü, Yuliyan, Woliyan, Da'aoye, and Ci'aoye; only the eldest escaped during the army turmoil. That Jin History form of Yuliyan is the same as this table's Yuliyan.
Literal likewise needs the 餘里衍/余里衍 equivalence without Chinese characters in the English field; Jin History vs table wording marks the variant note.
